sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>
sections.docs:
<docs>
Pi documentation (read only when the user asks about pi itself, its SDK, extensions, themes, skills, or TUI):
- Main documentation: <vol>/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/README.md
- Additional docs: <vol>/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs
- Examples: <vol>/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/examples (extensions, custom tools, SDK)
- When reading pi docs or examples, resolve docs/... under Additional docs and examples/... under Examples, not the current working directory
- When asked about: extensions (docs/extensions.md, examples/extensions/), themes (docs/themes.md), skills (docs/skills.md), prompt templates (docs/prompt-templates.md), TUI components (docs/tui.md), keybindings (docs/keybindings.md), SDK integrations (docs/sdk.md), custom providers (docs/custom-provider.md), adding models (docs/models.md), pi packages (docs/packages.md), environment variables (docs/environment-variables.md), MCP servers (docs/mcp.md), codemode scripts and non-LLM models such as classifiers and image models (docs/codemode.md)
- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.
I'll start by exploring the current directory.

# Surfing Pelican

An endless, non-interactive summer glide: a pelican on a surfboard, riding an
open-ocean swell into a low sunset sun, cut together like a little surf film.

No interaction, no controls — it just plays, forever.

Open `index.html` and it runs. Everything on screen is generated in code: the
swell, the sky, the sun, the clouds, the pelican, the surfboard, the spray.
There are no image, model or audio assets and no network requests.

```bash
npm install          # installs three
# then serve the folder however you like, e.g.
npx esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=bundle.js
```

## What you see

* **The ocean** is a "projected" polar grid that follows the surfer: rings are
  half a unit apart under the board and stretch out to 6 km at the horizon, so
  the sea never runs out but stays dense where the camera is. Displacement
  happens in the vertex shader; normals, whitecaps, sun glitter, sky reflection
  and haze are evaluated per pixel.
* **The swell** is five superimposed sine waves. The *same* table drives the
  GLSL that moves the water and the JavaScript that floats the board
  (`js/waves.js` emits the shader source), so the surfer really does ride the
  surface you see.
* **The pelican** is built from primitives and extruded shapes — no meshes are
  loaded. It pumps through the faces, banks into the turns, drags a wing in the
  foam now and then, and throws a rooster tail of spray.
* **The camera** cuts between six shots (chase, side, water-level, top, front,
  wide) on a loop, dipping to black across each cut.
* Around it: gulls wheeling overhead, low-poly islands on the haze line, and
  the sun sitting on the water.

## Files

| file | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `index.html` | entry point: canvas, fade overlay, title |
| `main.js` | renderer, lights, scene graph, frame loop |
| `styles.css` | page chrome + title fade |
| `js/palette.js` | every colour in the scene, in one place |
| `js/waves.js` | the swell (JS + generated GLSL) |
| `js/ocean.js` | water grid + water shader |
| `js/sky.js` | sky dome, sun and clouds |
| `js/pelican.js` | the pelican, the surfboard and the riding animation |
| `js/spray.js` | particle spray |
| `js/flock.js` | gulls |
| `js/islands.js` | horizon islands (recycled as you travel) |
| `js/contact.js` | soft contact shadow on the water |
| `js/camera.js` | the self-editing shot list |
| `tools/` | dev-only helpers (see below) |

## Dev helpers

`tools/` contains optional helpers used to check the scene without a display:
they bundle `main.js` the way the shipped page is bundled, render it in
headless Chrome (software WebGL) and write screenshots. They are not needed by
the page and need two extra dev dependencies:

```bash
npm i -D puppeteer pngjs
node tools/shoot.mjs 5 15 23 31 38 47   # screenshot specific timeline points
node tools/sample.mjs 31                # print a grid of pixel values
node tools/playback.mjs                 # watch a live run for errors
```

`window.__pelican` in the console exposes `seek(seconds)` to jump to a point on
the timeline, plus the rider, camera rig and ocean uniforms for poking at.

## Notes

* Colours are authored as sRGB hex and converted to the linear working space;
  the custom shaders finish with `linearToOutputTexel()` so custom and built-in
  materials agree.
* Nothing is stored (no `localStorage`, cookies or storage APIs), no fonts,
  images or data are fetched — the page is happy in a sandboxed iframe with the
  network switched off.

## Dev helpers

`tools/` contains optional helpers used to check the scene without a display:
they bundle `main.js` the way the shipped page is bundled, render it in
headless Chrome (software WebGL) and write screenshots. They are not needed by
the page and need two extra dev dependencies:

```bash
npm i -D puppeteer pngjs
node tools/shoot.mjs 5 15 23 31 38 47   # screenshot specific timeline points
node tools/sample.mjs 31                # print a grid of pixel values
node tools/playback.mjs                 # watch a live run for errors
```

`window.__pelican` in the console exposes `seek(seconds)` to jump to a point on
the timeline, plus the rider, camera rig and ocean uniforms for poking at.

## Notes

* Colours are authored as sRGB hex and converted to the linear working space;
  the custom shaders finish with `linearToOutputTexel()` so custom and built-in
  materials agree.
* Nothing is stored (no `localStorage`, cookies or storage APIs), no fonts,
  images or data are fetched — the page is happy in a sandboxed iframe with the
  network switched off.

content.text:
## What I built

**Surfing Pelican** — a non-interactive, endless animated scene in `index.html` + ES modules + three.js.

**The scene**
- **Ocean**: a polar "projected grid" that follows the surfer — half-metre rings under the board stretching to 6 km at the horizon, so the sea never ends but stays dense where the camera is. Vertex shader displacement, per-pixel normals, whitecaps on steep crests, sun glitter, fresnel sky reflection, and haze.
- **The swell**: five superimposed sines in one table (`js/waves.js`) that *generates its own GLSL*, so the water mesh and the floating board are guaranteed to agree — the pelican really rides the surface you see.
- **The pelican**: modelled from primitives and extruded shapes (no assets) — long hooked beak with a hanging pouch, tapered neck with a red bandana collar, vertex-coloured wings with dark tips, webbed feet on a striped board with rocker, fins and a tail fin. It pumps through the faces, banks into turns, flaps lazily, and throws a rooster-tail of particle spray.
- **Around it**: sunset sky dome with sun disc/god-rays and drifting fbm clouds, gulls wheelling overhead, low-poly islands recycled on the haze line, a soft contact shadow, and a **self-editing camera** cutting between six shots (chase / side / water-level / top / front / wide) with dips to black.

**Verification** — I installed headless Chrome (SwiftShader WebGL) and rendered the real bundled page repeatedly to check it: fixed a GLSL `vec2.z` swizzle error, a subject-framing bug that pushed the rider to the bottom of every shot, a wake halo that read as a milky wash, and an over-strong "sky ambient" term (linear-space values aren't sRGB values). The final six shots were each eyeballed from screenshots. `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` succeeds; playback shows no NaNs, no console errors, and correct shot cuts.

`tools/` holds the dev-only screenshot/pixel/playback helpers (documented in the README, need `npm i -D puppeteer pngjs`); they're not used by the page. No network requests, no storage APIs, no asset URLs.
